clue.text: Fellow hugging the Parisian tree

indicators.note: to hug is to wrap your arms round something, so one piece wraps round another

parts.note: a fellow is a man, a male

explanation.surface: A man throwing his arms round a tree in Paris.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Parisian' is the usual way to ask for a French definite article; the masculine one is wanted here.
explanation.definitionFit: A mallee is a scrubby Australian eucalyptus with several stems growing from one rootstock.

clue.text: Mineral from Spanish region found in mine, bottom of mine

indicators.note: something found inside another thing sits within it, so one piece is placed inside

parts.note: a pit is a coal mine
Aragon is a region of north-east Spain

indicators.note: in a down entry the bottom of a word is its final letter

parts.note: the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A mineral dug from a Spanish mine, perhaps at the bottom of the shaft.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mine' is used twice: once as a whole word, once only for its last letter. Aragon was a medieval kingdom, now an autonomous region.
explanation.definitionFit: Paragonite is a sodium-bearing mica, a rock-forming silicate found in schists.

clue.text: Goods trendy chaps dumped in street

indicators.note: things dumped in a place end up inside it, so one piece goes within another

explanation.surface: Fashionable young men abandoned on the street with their goods.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dumped' suggests the goods were thrown away, but it only places the trendy chaps inside the street.
explanation.definitionFit: A shipment is a consignment of merchandise sent together, so it can stand for goods.

clue.text: Container housing a paper garment

indicators.note: a building housing something holds it inside, so one piece is held within another

parts.note: the Financial Times, a British newspaper

explanation.surface: A box holding a newspaper and a piece of clothing.
explanation.walkthrough: CAN holds A and FT. FT is the Financial Times, the pink British business daily.
explanation.definitionFit: A caftan is a long loose tunic of Middle Eastern origin, an item of clothing.

clue.text: Column has one Scottish flower put up in club maybe

indicators.note: placing something in another thing puts it inside

parts.note: a club is one suit of playing card

indicators.note: in a down entry, putting something up lifts it so it reads bottom to top

parts.note: a 'flower' is a river, something that flows; the Tay is Scotland's longest

explanation.surface: A pillar decorated with a Scottish bloom hoisted up in a golf club.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flower' is the crossword trick for a river, something that flows. 'Club' is not a golf club or nightclub but a playing-card suit.
explanation.definitionFit: A caryatid is a carved female figure that serves as a supporting pillar in classical architecture.

clue.text: Ruined female occupying one outbuilding

parts.note: occupying a place is being in it
a shed is a small outbuilding

explanation.surface: A woman left wrecked, living in a garden shed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Occupying' looks like a container signal, but here it simply supplies IN in a plain run of pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone finished is done for, beyond rescue, which is what ruined means.

clue.text: Has she exploded, having swallowed explosive drug?

indicators.note: what is swallowed ends up inside, so one piece goes within the other
something blown apart lands in pieces, so these letters are scattered and rearranged

explanation.surface: A worried question about a woman who has blown up after swallowing a dangerous drug.
explanation.walkthrough: The jumbled letters take in the explosive after their third letter. HE, high explosive, is a standard abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Hasheesh is a variant spelling of hashish, the cannabis resin, so it is a narcotic.

clue.text: Irishman taking a very long time to cross island

indicators.note: to cross something is to span it, so one piece stretches across and round another

parts.note: an eon is an immensely long period

explanation.surface: An Irishman taking ages to get across an island.
explanation.walkthrough: EON goes round I.
explanation.definitionFit: Eoin is the Irish form of the name John, so it is a typical Irish man's name.

clue.text: See 16
One beating old age — ran twice!

definitions.text: One beating old age — ran twice!

indicators.note: beating something knocks it about, so these letters are battered into a new order

parts.note: the word written out two times

explanation.surface: Praise for someone who outran old age, and did so twice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Twice' tells you to use RAN two times. The whole clue doubles as the definition: Reagan, elected at 69 and again at 73, ran for president twice despite his age.
explanation.definitionFit: Reagan was then the oldest man elected US president and won two terms, defying age at the ballot box.

clue.text: Plant physics unit in e.g. Dorset

indicators.note: placing something in another thing puts it inside

parts.note: Dorset is an English county, a shire
the ampere, the unit of electric current

explanation.surface: A plant used in physics research somewhere in Dorset.
explanation.walkthrough: Dorset is a county on England's south coast, and shire is an old word for county; 'e.g.' marks it as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: Samphire is a fleshy coastal plant, eaten as a vegetable and found on Dorset's shores.

clue.text: Useful home device when a person is out

indicators.note: something that is out is out of place or wrong, so these letters need putting in a new order

explanation.surface: A handy gadget for when nobody is home.
explanation.walkthrough: It reads like a cryptic definition, and works as one, but 'when a person' has exactly the right letters. 'Answerphone' is the British name for an answering machine.
explanation.definitionFit: An answering machine records incoming telephone messages whenever the householder is away and cannot pick up.

clue.text: Model wasting time with friend acting as old man

indicators.note: to waste something is to throw it away, so a letter is lost

parts.note: a pattern is a model to copy

explanation.surface: A model idling with a friend who plays the part of an older man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Model' suggests a fashion model, but it is a template to copy. 'Old man' is slang for father, so the definition is an adverb of manner.
explanation.definitionFit: To act paternally is to behave in the manner of a father, and 'old man' is informal for one's dad.

clue.text: Ancient weapon with which a Scottish detective protects Queen

indicators.note: a guard protects by surrounding, so one piece wraps round another

parts.note: Inspector Rebus is Ian Rankin's Edinburgh detective
QU is an abbreviation for queen

explanation.surface: A detective guarding the monarch with an old-fashioned gun.
explanation.walkthrough: Inspector Rebus is the hero of Ian Rankin's Edinburgh crime novels, a staple of British TV and bookshops.
explanation.definitionFit: The arquebus was an early portable matchlock firearm of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries.

clue.text: Star about to confront theologian, fighting fellow

explanation.surface: A celebrity about to square up to a divine, the two fellows coming to blows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Star' suggests a celebrity, and Red Dwarf is also a British TV sitcom, but here it is the astronomical object.
explanation.definitionFit: A red dwarf is a small, cool, faint star, the most common type in our galaxy.

clue.text: Repeating liturgy, first to last, with a part of the Bible

indicators.note: moving the opening letter round to the end rotates the word

parts.note: a rite is a form of liturgy

explanation.surface: Reciting the liturgy and a passage of scripture over and over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Repeating' could be a verb, but the answer is an adjective, so read it as describing something that repeats.
explanation.definitionFit: Iterant is a rare adjective meaning repetitive, from iterate, to do again and again.

clue.text: Sick, beset by pains, the chap with little energy left showing fatal weakness

indicators.note: to be beset is to be surrounded on all sides, so one piece is enclosed

parts.note: E is the symbol for energy, a small piece of it

explanation.surface: A sick man in pain with barely any energy left, showing a mortal frailty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left' looks like 'remaining' but is just the abbreviation L; 'little energy' is its one-letter symbol.
explanation.definitionFit: Achilles was invulnerable except at his heel, so the phrase names a single fatal vulnerability.

clue.text: As orderly patients may be dealt with, said US medical student

indicators.note: something said is spoken, so we go by the sound of the words

parts.words: As orderly patients may be dealt with
parts.note: patients seen in an orderly way are dealt with one after another

explanation.surface: A trainee doctor at an American hospital seeing patients in an orderly queue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Orderly' looks like a hospital attendant, but here it describes the way patients are seen: in turn.
explanation.definitionFit: An interne, also spelt intern, is a recent medical graduate training in a US hospital.

clue.text: Behave frivolously, ditching what could be hard and onerous

indicators.note: this asks what the letters could become if rearranged
to ditch something is to drop it, so a word in the clue is thrown out

parts.note: the joining word itself, which is the part thrown out

explanation.surface: Someone fooling about to escape tough, burdensome work.
explanation.walkthrough: The fodder is 'hard and onerous' with the word AND dropped, so only HARD ONEROUS is rearranged. 'And' looks like a plain joining word but it is the thing ditched.
explanation.definitionFit: To horse around is an informal idiom for messing about or playing the fool.

clue.text: See 9 Across
One companion and another having hesitation

parts.note: another companion: CH is Companion of Honour, a British order
um is a sound of hesitation

explanation.surface: Two friends, one of whom keeps stalling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Another' means another companion, here the CH of Companion of Honour, an honour awarded by the British monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: A chum is a close friend, an informal word for a pal or mate.

clue.text: English and American soldiers providing protection in Washington

explanation.surface: British and US troops guarding the American capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In Washington' flags the American spelling, without the A of aegis.
explanation.definitionFit: Egis is the US spelling of aegis, a shield or sponsorship that shelters someone.

clue.text: The fellow surprisingly genial as a philosopher

indicators.note: something surprising is unexpected, so the letters come out in an unexpected order

explanation.surface: A man who turns out to be unexpectedly friendly for a thinker.
explanation.walkthrough: HE is followed by a rearranged GENIAL.
explanation.definitionFit: A Hegelian is a follower of the German thinker Hegel, so is a kind of philosopher.

clue.text: Brazilian dance seeing off a Greek character

indicators.note: to see someone off is to get rid of them, so a letter goes

parts.note: the lambada is a dance from Brazil

explanation.surface: A dancer from Brazil chasing away a Greek.
explanation.walkthrough: LAMBADA loses one A.
explanation.definitionFit: Lambda is the eleventh letter of the Greek alphabet, the equivalent of L.

clue.text: Skilful mum unsmilingly disposing of last of children

indicators.note: to dispose of something is to get rid of it, so a letter is removed
the last of a word is its final letter

parts.note: the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: An expert mother grimly getting rid of her youngest child.
explanation.walkthrough: MA is followed by STERNLY minus N, the last letter of 'children'.
explanation.definitionFit: Masterly means performed with the expertise of a master, highly accomplished.

clue.text: Some rock in church service, followed by a poem

parts.note: Mass is the Catholic church service

explanation.surface: Some rock music played during Mass, with a poem read afterwards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some rock' suggests rock music; it is a lump of mountain. Kipling's If— is one of the best-known poems in English.
explanation.definitionFit: A massif is a compact group of mountains, a large mass of rock in geology.
